Article.ArticleTitle: Comparison of two close-packing methods for vertex placement in lattice radiotherapy (LRT).

Abstract.AbstractText: Lattice Radiation Therapy (LRT) is characterized by its 3D-mouldated spatial dose distribution of vertices inside the lattice volume with high peak-to-valley dose ratio (PVDR) for enhancing tumor control and reducing normal tissue toxicity. While face-centered cubic (FCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP), both achieving maximum spatial packing density, have been used for vertex placement, a direct comparative analysis of their dosimetric performance is lacking.

This study aimed to systematically compare FCC and HCP methods for vertex placement under identical conditions to determine which yields superior dosimetric outcomes, specifically regarding the peak-to-valley dose ratio (PVDR), and to provide data supporting the standardization of LRT planning.

This study was retrospectively conducted on 10 patients with large gross tumor volumes (GTV) (GTV; median [IQR] GTV volume: 916.59[609.37] cm3). For each patient, an identical inward margin was applied to the GTV to create the lattice volume for placing LRT vertices. Within this lattice volume, two sets of spherical vertices were generated: one arranged in a HCP lattice and the other in a FCC lattice, both vertices of same diameter. The initial diameter and volume of vertices were determined based on GTV volume. Vertex positions were optimized using an Adaptive Simulated Annealing (ASA) algorithm to maximize inter-vertex distance, with the total volume of all vertices constrained to approximately 1% of the GTV. All plans were optimized using identical dose-volume objectives. Plan quality was evaluated using GTV dose metrics (D5%, D10%, D50%, D90%, Dmean, V50%), normal tissue mean dose (NT Dmean), maximum point doses (Dmax) to serial organs at risk and PVDR defined by both GTVD10/D90 and lattice volume D10/D90 ratios.

Vertex parameters (number, volume, spacing) showed no significant difference between Plan_FCC and Plan_HCP (P > 0.05). Dosimetric analysis revealed a statistically significant increase in PVDR (lattice volume D10/D90) for Plan_FCC compared to Plan_HCP (median [IQR]: 6.95 [3.38] vs. 4.48 [2.00], p = 0.019). No other evaluated metrics demonstrated significant differences, including other GTV metrics NT Dmean or the maximum point doses to serial OARs.

Under matched radiation delivery technique, geometric constraints and identical dose-volume objectives, the FCC vertex arrangement yields a statistically significantly higher peak-to-valley dose ratio (lattice volume D10/D90), compared to the HCP arrangement, without compromising other dosimetric indices. This finding suggests that FCC may be a preferred starting configuration for LRT vertex placement in large tumors and we recommend that the FCC arrangement be prioritized in clinical practice.

Article.ArticleTitle: Dissecting the Radioresponse Heterogeneity of Lung Adenocarcinoma Cells From the Perspective of Transcriptional and Regulatory Landscape.

Abstract.AbstractText: Radioresistance severely compromises radiotherapy efficacy for lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), yet the intrinsic heterogeneity of cellular radioresponses among isogenic tumor cells remains poorly characterized. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing (scATAC-seq) to dissect the transcriptional and regulatory landscape underlying heterogeneous radioresponses in single-cell-derived LUAD cells following 6 Gy γ-ray irradiation. We found that isogenic LUAD cells harbored intrinsic molecular determinants for divergent radiosensitivity and displayed heterogeneous radioresponsiveness upon irradiation. A radiation-associated transcriptional cell state, coupled with DNA damage repair, apoptosis, and cell cycle regulation, emerged at 6 h post-irradiation. Inhibition of lysine demethylase 4B (KDM4B) enhanced LUAD radiosensitivity by intensifying DNA damage, whereas reduced expression of cyclin B1 (CCNB1) and DNA topoisomerase IIα (TOP2A) potentially contributed to radiation-triggered G2/M arrest. Notably, the radiation-associated regulatory cell state emerged earlier than radiation-induced transcriptional cell state. RNA polymerase II subunit A (POLR2A) functioned as a core regulator in high-responsive LUAD cells. Based on these findings, we proposed a hypothesis for the radiosensitization of LUAD cells. Collectively, this study provides multilayer mechanistic insights into LUAD radioresponse heterogeneity and yields actionable molecular candidates for developing improved radiosensitization strategies to advance precise radiotherapy for LUAD.

Article.ArticleTitle: Radiobiological dosimetry using hybrid imaging-derived spatiotemporal dose distributions for131I therapy of metastatic thyroid cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Objective.To develop a patient-specific radiobiological dosimetry framework that incorporates temporal dose delivery and spatial heterogeneity using hybrid imaging for131I therapy of metastatic thyroid cancer.Approach.Four-dimensional particle source distributions were reconstructed for eight adults from one quantitative pretherapy single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography acquisition and three serial planar images. An in-house Monte Carlo engine transported the sources through each patient's computed tomography geometry and scored absorbed dose in 1 h bins for 23 lesions. Voxelwise Lea-Catcheside repair factors and biologically effective dose (BED) were calculated from the temporal dose profiles, followed by lesion-level equivalent uniform BED (EUBED) and tumor control probability (TCP). The administered activity required to achieve 50% TCP (TCA50) was calculated under no, partial, and complete sublethal damage repair. Tumor repopulation was evaluated separately, and sensitivity analysis of the radiobiological parameters assessed their effects on TCA50.Main results.Predicted tumor control varied substantially across and within patients and depended on lesion-specific dose distributions and the assumed radiobiological parameters. Of the parameters varied from 0.5 to 1.5 times baseline, the linear radiosensitivity coefficienthad the greatest effect on TCA50. Median TCA50values were 6.99, 14.38, and 15.02 GBq under no, partial, and complete repair, respectively. SmallG-factors (median, 0.0133) resulted in partial-repair TCP curves and TCA50estimates close to those under complete repair. Increasing activity amplified spatial BED heterogeneity and produced sublinear increases in EUBED, indicating that prescriptions based only on mean absorbed dose or mean BED may overestimate treatment effectiveness. Temporal TCP trajectories revealed changes in predicted control during tumor repopulation that were not captured by endpoint TCP alone.Significance.The proposed framework enables patient-specific voxelwise radiobiological modeling through TCP using one quantitative SPECT/CT acquisition and serial planar imaging. It may support biologically informed activity prescription, although its model-dependent predictions require clinical validation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Combined PET imaging of tumor hypoxia and proliferation in Glioblastoma using a single injection of 18F-FMISO and 18F-FLT: Association with sites of subsequent recurrence.

Abstract.AbstractText: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intra-tumoral heterogeneity, rapid proliferation, hypoxia-driven radio-resistance, and early recurrence. Gadolinium-Enhanced MRI, the standard of care imaging modality for surgical and radiotherapy planning, lacks specificity for viable tumor burden, particularly in non-enhancing regions.

This pilot study aimed to evaluate whether preoperative dual-tracer PET using a combined dose of 18FMISO (hypoxia) and 18FLT (proliferation) improves tumor delineation and predicts subsequent local recurrence compared with MRI.

Seven patients with WHO grade 4 gliomas (5 GBM, 2 IDH-mutant astrocytomas) underwent preoperative dual-[FMISO+FLT] static PET at 180 min post-injection, and MRI. 6/7 patients underwent resection. Tumor volumes were segmented from PET, contrast-enhanced T1 (T1-Gd), and T2-FLAIR. Postoperative resection cavities were delineated, and follow-up MRI every 3 months was used to identify recurrence. PET-defined tumor volumes extending beyond resection were correlated with subsequent recurrence sites.

Thirteen lesions were analyzed; all showed [FMISO+FLT] uptake (mean activity concentration ratio 1.6 with the cerebellar cortex used as reference region). PET-defined tumor volumes (9.2 cc) were slightly larger than T1-Gd (7.9 cc) but smaller than T2-FLAIR (28.8 cc). PET-defined volumes frequently extended beyond MRI-defined contours (mean non-overlap 6.4 cc vs T1-Gd; 1.5 cc vs. T2-FLAIR). Of six patients undergoing resection, four developed local recurrence within 3.3 months. In all cases, recurrence arose within PET-avid regions outside the resection cavity. The other two patients with complete resection of PET-defined volumes showed a relatively prolonged progression-free-survival (PFS) and including one patient with overall survival exceeding 36 months.

Dual-[FMISO+FLT] PET is feasible, safe, and can allow delineation of biologically viable tumor subregions, in particular within the MRI T2-FLAIR volume. This approach prospectively identified sites of subsequent local recurrence and may improve surgical planning and radiotherapy dose escalation. Larger validation studies are warranted to establish dual-tracer PET as a precision imaging paradigm in GBM.

Article.ArticleTitle: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: During lung cancer radiotherapy, inter-fractional anatomical changes may cause the delivered dose to deviate from the primary plan, affecting tumor control and increasing the risk of normal tissue damage. This study aims to evaluate the impact of anatomical changes on the dosimetric and radiobiological performance of simulated proton arc therapy (sPAT) versus intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) for lung cancer patients under patient-specific anatomical changes.

Data from 21 lung cancer patients were retrospectively analyzed. The prescribed dose for all patients was 6000 cGy (relative biological effectiveness, RBE). Each patient with a primary planning computed tomography (pCT) and a mid-treatment adaptive-planning CT (aCT) acquired at a median of 29 days into treatment due to notable tumor volume changes. Primary plans for sPAT and IMPT were designed on the pCT. After rigid registration of the pCT and aCT, non-adaptive plans (sPATp-a, IMPTp-a) were generated by directly recalculating the doses of the primary plans on the aCT. The comparison evaluated the dosimetric impact of anatomical changes by comparing non-adaptive plans (sPATp-a vs. IMPTp-a). Dose-volume histogram (DVH) parameters for targets and organs at risk (OARs) and tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) were evaluated.

For the primary plans, sPAT and IMPT achieved similar target coverage, while the doses to OARs were generally lower in sPATp. Under anatomical changes, both non-adaptive plans exhibited a decrease in target coverage, sPATp-a achieved a D95% of 5567.57 cGy[RBE] compared with 5423.33 cGy[RBE] for IMPTp-a (p < 0.001), indicating that sPAT better preserved target coverage. Compared with the primary plans, sPATp-a and IMPTp-a exhibited TCP reductions of 5.83% and 8.07%, respectively.
Compared with IMPT, sPAT exhibits enhanced robustness against inter-fractional anatomical changes occurring in lung-cancer radiotherapy.

Article.ArticleTitle: Octreotide-modified pH-responsive nanocomposites for ultrasound imaging-guided chemo-photothermal therapy of prostate cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Prostate cancer remains a major malignancy in men, and its clinical management is still limited by insufficient tumor-specific imaging, inefficient drug delivery, and suboptimal therapeutic efficacy. Herein, we developed an octreotide-modified, pH-responsive polymer-mineral hybrid nanoplatform, IDOCP@CC, for ultrasound imaging-guided chemo-photothermal therapy of prostate cancer. The nanocomposites were constructed by loading doxorubicin and IR825 into octreotide-conjugated PF127-PAsp polymeric micelles, followed by in situ CaCO3 mineralization. IDOCP@CC exhibited a spherical core-shell structure, an average hydrodynamic diameter of approximately 220 nm, positive surface charge, and high encapsulation efficiencies for doxorubicin and IR825 of 79.05% and 76.86%, respectively. Under weakly acidic conditions, IDOCP@CC promoted drug release and generated CO2 bubbles from the CaCO3 shell, resulting in enhanced B-mode and contrast-enhanced ultrasound signals. The nanocomposites also showed stable photothermal performance under 808 nm near-infrared irradiation and enhanced cellular uptake in PC3 cells. In vitro, IDOCP@CC combined with NIR irradiation markedly increased reactive oxygen species generation, induced apoptosis and cell death, inhibited migration and colony formation, and promoted immunogenic cell death-associated signals. In PC3 xenograft-bearing nude mice, IDOCP@CC accumulated efficiently in tumors, enhanced contrast-enhanced ultrasound imaging, elevated tumor temperature under NIR irradiation, achieved a tumor inhibition rate of 69%, reduced serum PSA levels, downregulated β-catenin expression, and showed no obvious systemic toxicity. These findings suggest that IDOCP@CC is a promising octreotide-modified and pH-responsive theranostic nanoplatform for ultrasound imaging-guided chemo-photothermal therapy of prostate cancer.

Article.ArticleTitle: Development and validation of hypoxic chambers combined with an oxygen diffusion model for controlled radiobiological experiments.

Abstract.AbstractText: Tumor hypoxia is a hallmark of cancer that drives radioresistance, metastasis and poor clinical outcomes.In vitromodeling of hypoxic conditions is therefore critical for understanding tumor biology and testing therapeutic strategies. Commercially available hypoxic chambers, while very efficient at maintaining atmospheric conditions of samples, are often not portable, unsuitable for irradiation experiments and have a significant cost. In this study, we developed and tested two in-house hypoxic chambers (a portable chamber and a glove chamber), combined with a 1-D oxygen diffusion model for performing and validating biological experiments under controlled hypoxic environment. The systems were validated under physiologically relevant oxygen conditions (0%-4% O2) through continuous monitoring using PICO-O2and LuminOX sensors integrated via Arduino/Bluetooth. A 1-D diffusion model based on Fick's law was developed, predicting the exposure time required to achieve a target oxygen concentration as a function of the medium height. For a full end-to-end test of the system, we conducted immunofluorescence analysis to verify the hypoxic status of the cells and we irradiated triple negative breast cancer cells (MDA-MB-231) with photons and protons at doses ranging from 2.5-12.5 Gy under normoxic (21% O2concentration) and hypoxic (4% O2concentration) conditions, followed by clonogenic survival assay to test the cytotoxicity and radioresistance. Our results showed the ability of both chambers to properly maintain the target oxygen levels and the 1D-diffusion model reproduced hypoxia establishment times with <5% deviation from direct measurements in the medium (PICO-O2). Immunofluorescence analysis confirmed effective induction of cellular hypoxia, evidenced by increased hypoxia-associated fluorescence and elevated hypoxia-inducible factors-1αexpression under hypoxic conditions compared with normoxia. Additional biological results confirmed hypoxia-induced morphological changes and increased radioresistance, with consistent survival outcomes across both chambers. Together, the two chamber designs and the diffusion model provide a low-cost system for studying hypoxia-induced radioresistancein vitro.

Article.ArticleTitle: Variability of the Relative Biological Effectiveness of Carbon Ions Among Human Cancer Cell Lines Under Clinically Relevant Irradiation Conditions.

Abstract.AbstractText: In Japan, carbon-ion radiotherapy treatment planning uses relative biological effectiveness (RBE) values derived from a single reference cell line. Accumulating evidence indicates that carbon-ion RBE varies among different cancers. However, the magnitude of this variability remains unclear owing to the heterogeneity of the experimental conditions among the studies. This study aimed to elucidate carbon-ion RBE variability across a large panel of human cancer cell lines using clinically relevant irradiation conditions and consistent clonogenic assay methods.

Clonogenic survival in 41 human cancer cell lines after X-ray or carbon-ion irradiation was analyzed. Carbon-ion irradiation was performed at the center of a 6-cm spread-out Bragg peak (290 MeV/nucleon; dose-averaged linear energy transfer, approximately 50 keV/μm). RBE values at doses corresponding to 10% and 50% survival (D10 and D50, respectively) were calculated and compared with population-representative RBE values derived by linear regression and with those of the reference human salivary gland (HSG) cell line.

Population-representative RBE values were 2.09 and 2.28 for D10 and D50, respectively, closely approximating those of HSG cells (1.92 and 2.37). However, approximately 32% of the cell lines exhibited RBE values that deviated by at least 24% from the population-representative values. This variability was greater for D50 than for D10. No association was found between RBE and primary organ or histological subtype.

Substantial inter-cell line RBE variability was observed under consistent and clinically relevant irradiation conditions, indicating that the current fixed-RBE approach contributes to potential overtreatment or undertreatment in a subset of patients.

Article.ArticleTitle: Abscopal-like Regression of Lung Metastases After Near-infrared Photoimmunotherapy Plus Nivolumab in Laryngeal Carcinoma.

Abstract.AbstractText: Near-infrared photoimmunotherapy (NIR-PIT) combines tumor-selective cytotoxicity with the induction of immunogenic cell death and may therefore augment the systemic activity of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). However, clinical evidence of responses in distant, non-illuminated lesions is lacking. We describe a distant visceral response following NIR-PIT administered during programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade.

A man in his 60s presented with recurrent laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma involving the base of the tongue and multiple pulmonary metastases that had progressed after definitive chemoradiotherapy, salvage total laryngectomy, re-irradiation, and platinum- and pembrolizumab-containing regimens. Nivolumab monotherapy was initiated, and NIR-PIT of the base-of-tongue lesion was added one month later. Using the pre-NIR-PIT status as baseline, the target pulmonary metastasis decreased from 12.1 to 8.0 mm and a cervical lymph node from 15.3 to 11.1 mm at 4 months (sum -30.3%; partial response by RECIST 1.1), with both lesions located outside the illuminated field. This response deepened and was maintained at 10 months (7.6 and 8.2 mm; sum -42.3%). In contrast, the illuminated base-of-tongue lesion persisted despite a second NIR-PIT at 5 months. Adverse events were limited to grade 2 facial and cervical edema and local pain.

The addition of local NIR-PIT to nivolumab was followed by durable, abscopal-like regression of non-illuminated pulmonary metastases in immunotherapy-refractory head and neck cancer. While causality cannot be established from a single case, this observation supports formal investigation of NIR-PIT-ICI combinations in patients with distant metastases.

Article.ArticleTitle: Differences in Biological Responses to Ultra-high Dose Rate Proton Irradiation Between Entrance and SOBP Regions In Vitro.

Abstract.AbstractText: Ultra-high dose rate (FLASH) radiotherapy has been reported to reduce normal tissue toxicity while maintaining tumor control. However, whether proton FLASH induces different biological responses in the entrance versus spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) regions under controlled irradiation conditions remains unclear. This study compared biological responses to ultra-high dose rate proton irradiation in the entrance and SOBP regions at matched dose and time-averaged dose rate conditions.

Non-tumor V79 Chinese hamster lung fibroblasts cells were irradiated with 230 MeV protons using pencil beam scanning under hypoxic (1% O2) conditions. Dose-rate conditions of 1, 40, and 100 Gy/s were applied for entrance irradiation, and 1 and 100 Gy/s for SOBP irradiation. The surviving fraction was analyzed using a clonogenic cell survival assay.

Clonogenic survival decreased dose-dependently at all dose rates. In the entrance region, no consistent dose-rate differences were observed up to 21 Gy; at 24 Gy, 100 Gy/s yielded a significantly higher surviving fraction than 1 Gy/s. In the SOBP region, the surviving fraction did not differ significantly between 1 and 100 Gy/s at 24 Gy.

Under controlled conditions, a significant dose-rate-associated difference in clonogenic survival was observed in the entrance region at 24 Gy but not in the SOBP region. Further studies are required to determine whether the dose rate effect differs according to irradiation depth.

Article.ArticleTitle: Impact of robust optimization and beam configuration on the distribution stability of LET under delivery uncertainties in carbon-ion therapy.

Abstract.AbstractText: Carbon-ion radiotherapy exploits high linear energy transfer (LET) to enhance biological effectiveness, and low dose-averaged LET (LETd) within the target volume is associated with local recurrence in pancreatic cancer. Although robust optimization is widely used to improve dose robustness against delivery uncertainties, systematic investigation of LET robustness across optimization strategies and beam configurations remains scarce.

To evaluate the robustness of LET metrics in carbon-ion therapy under delivery uncertainties using a phantom-based design, comparing planning target volume (PTV)-based with robust optimization and assessing the impact of seven beam configurations, and to characterize the differential response of LET and clinical dose (relative biological effectiveness [RBE]-weighted dose) metrics.

A 30 × 30 × 30 cm3 water-equivalent phantom with rod- and C-shaped target geometries was planned in RayStation 12A with 50 Gy (RBE) in 10 fractions. Section 1 used two opposing lateral fields to compare PTV-based optimization (1, 3, 5 mm margins) with robust optimization incorporating translation, density, and combined uncertainties. Section 2 evaluated seven beam configurations, ranging from two-field to four-field arrangements, under PTV-based (3 mm) and robust (± 3%/3 mm) optimization. LETd98%, LETd mean, and LETd2% were extracted for the clinical target volume and organs at risk (OARs). Robustness was quantified using averaged interquartile range (AVG.IQR) and sensitivity slopes from 1% to 5% density uncertainty (S1→5), and configurations were ranked by minimal-change and biologically favorable criteria. Spot weight distributions were analyzed to examine the mechanistic basis of the observed differences.

Density-related uncertainties dominated LET variability, with LETd2% the most sensitive metric (AVG.IQR up to 40% for C-shaped targets). Robust optimization with combined translation-density parameters achieved lower variability than PTV-based optimization. LET and RBE-weighted dose metrics responded divergently, with the LETd mean increasing while the mean clinical dose decreased under density perturbations. Beam direction significantly affected LETd2% variability (p < 0.001 for all configurations). Two lateral fields (2Lat) ranked highest under the minimal-change criterion, whereas four-field oblique (4FO) with robust optimization ranked first under the biologically favorable criterion, balancing increased target LET against reduced OAR exposure. Spot weight analysis showed that, for the rod-shaped target, only robustness scenarios including density uncertainty used more energy layers and shifted weight away from distal layers (distal-third weight fraction 56.4-57.4% vs. 60.8% for PTV-based optimization); this pattern was not reproduced for the C-shaped target.

Density uncertainties predominantly govern LET variability in carbon-ion therapy, with LETd2% the most sensitive indicator, and redistribution of spot weight away from distal energy layers provides a plausible mechanism. Beam configuration selection should reflect clinical priorities: 4FO with robust optimization when biological effectiveness is prioritized, and 2Lat for physical LET stability. These phantom-based findings support explicit LET robustness evaluation in carbon-ion treatment planning and warrant validation in patient studies.

Journal.Title: Journal of photochemistry and photobiology. B, Biology

Article.ArticleTitle: Cisplatin@nZIF-8 nanoparticles enable NIR-assisted drug release and ROS-mediated DNA damage for enhanced chemotherapy against triple-negative breast cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains heavily reliant on chemotherapy; however, the clinical use of cisplatin is constrained by systemic toxicity, particularly nephrotoxicity. In this study, cisplatin-loaded nanoscale ZIF-8 nanoparticles (Cisplatin@nZIF-8) were developed as a pH-responsive, 808 nm near-infrared (NIR)-assisted delivery platform for MDA-MB-436 TNBC cells. Following cisplatin loading, the particle size increased from 152 ± 8 to 196 ± 10 nm, the hydrodynamic diameter expanded from 343 ± 6 to 571 ± 11 nm, the zeta potential shifted from +23.4 to -20.5 mV, and the BET surface area decreased from 1993.751 to 1567.185 m2/g, confirming the successful incorporation of cisplatin within or onto the porous ZIF-8 framework. The loading efficiency was approximately 41%, equivalent to 2.05 ± 0.86 μg cisplatin per mg nZIF-8. Cisplatin@nZIF-8 exhibited greater drug release at pH 5.5 than at pH 7.4, consistent with its acid-responsive release behavior. Upon 808 nm NIR irradiation at 2 W/cm2 for 10 min, Cisplatin@nZIF-8 generated a concentration-dependent mild photothermal response. At 100 μg/mL, the temperature increased by 7.2 °C-7.6 °C, corresponding to a net rise of 3.7 °C-4.1 °C after background correction. In MDA-MB-436 cells, NIR irradiation further enhanced the cytotoxic activity of Cisplatin@nZIF-8, while repeated irradiation at 0 and 48 h produced greater growth inhibition at 72 h than a single irradiation treatment. This enhanced anticancer activity was accompanied by increased intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and elevated DNA strand breaks, indicating that NIR-assisted treatment aggravated downstream cisplatin-associated DNA damage. In HEK-293 kidney-derived cells, Cisplatin@nZIF-8 demonstrated a more favorable cytotoxicity profile than free cisplatin. Collectively, Cisplatin@nZIF-8 combines acid-responsive cisplatin release, mild NIR-assisted heating, ROS-associated cellular damage, and enhanced DNA strand break formation, improving cisplatin-mediated TNBC treatment while reducing toxicity toward renal cells.

Journal.Title: Journal of applied clinical medical physics

Article.ArticleTitle: Vision and implementation for the first U.S. carbon ion therapy center part I: Clinical rationale and the need for CIRT in the United States.

Abstract.AbstractText: Carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) has evolved into an established clinical modality over the past three decades. Owing to its unique physical and biological characteristics, CIRT has demonstrated favorable outcomes for selected malignancies characterized by radioresistance, proximity to critical organs, locally advanced disease requiring safe dose escalation, and recurrent tumors requiring re-irradiation. This review summarizes the physical and radiobiological rationale for CIRT, the evolution of international clinical practice and the clinical relative biological effectiveness models and dose prescription systems currently used in Asia and Europe. We discuss the differences between the modified microdosimetric kinetic model and Local Effect Model frameworks and their implications for interpreting and applying international clinical experience. We also describe the biological dose calculation framework adopted by Mayo Clinic Florida (MCF) to integrate established international CIRT experience into the first U.S. program. Published estimates of CIRT eligibility and need in the United States are reviewed to provide context for the anticipated U.S. patient population. This population includes many clinically complex disease sites characterized by proximity to critical organs, respiratory motion, anatomical variation, and the potential need for adaptive treatment. These clinical characteristics define important requirements for the first U.S. CIRT program and provide the foundation for the design philosophy and technical implementation described in the companion Part II article.

Article.ArticleTitle: Protein Lactylation in Cancer: From Mechanisms to Therapy.

Abstract.AbstractText: Protein lactylation has emerged as a metabolically responsive posttranslational modification linking lactate accumulation to epigenetic and functional adaptation in cancer. Initially identified on histones, lactylation is now recognized on diverse nonhistone proteins involved in DNA damage repair, immune regulation, redox homeostasis, metabolic remodeling, and cellular plasticity. However, current evidence remains fragmented across treatment modalities, and many reported lactylation events lack site-specific functional validation and translational assessment. This review addresses this gap by integrating the metabolic and enzymatic basis of protein lactylation with its roles in chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. We critically examine how lactylation may promote tumor persistence under therapeutic pressure by enhancing genome maintenance, immune evasion, stress-survival signaling, metabolic adaptability, and tumor microenvironment remodeling. We also evaluate emerging strategies targeting lactate production and transport, lactylation-regulating enzymes, and functionally validated substrates, including their potential use in combination therapies. Finally, we discuss major barriers to clinical translation, including incomplete characterization of regulatory enzymes, limitations in site-specific lactylome mapping, insufficient causal validation, lack of clinically qualified biomarkers, tumor metabolic heterogeneity, and challenges in achieving therapeutic selectivity. Collectively, protein lactylation represents an emerging mechanistic framework for understanding cancer treatment adaptation and a potentially targetable axis whose clinical relevance requires rigorous validation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Baicalein enhances radiosensitivity in cervical cancer by targeting ALOX15 and regulating lipid metabolism.

Abstract.AbstractText: Radiotherapy is the mainstay for locally advanced cervical cancer, but its efficacy is compromised by radioresistance. Dysregulated lipid metabolism contributes to therapeutic resistance, offering a promising strategy to improve radiosensitivity. This study aimed to explore the effect and mechanism of baicalein in enhancing radiosensitivity of cervical cancer cells. In vitro experiments were performed to assess the radiosensitizing effect of baicalein, while potential targets were identified through bioinformatics and network pharmacology. The key target was further validated by gene knockdown, and in vivo experiments were conducted to confirm the effects of baicalein combined with radiotherapy. ALOX15 was identified as a key target of baicalein, and high ALOX15 expression was associated with poor prognosis in cervical cancer. Both baicalein treatment and ALOX15 suppression enhanced radiosensitivity, reduced lipid droplet accumulation, and downregulated the SREBP1/FASN/ACC protein expression. In vivo, baicalein combined with radiotherapy reduced lipid accumulation and serum lipid levels, with effects comparable to those of the ALOX15 inhibitor AA861. Collectively, these findings suggest that baicalein enhances radiosensitivity in cervical cancer by targeting ALOX15 and modulating lipid metabolism via the SREBP1/FASN/ACC pathway. ALOX15 may be a potential regulator of radioresistance, and baicalein warrants further investigation as a potential radiosensitizer.

Article.ArticleTitle: A multimode radiobiological model for advanced radiation therapy.

Abstract.AbstractText: Reliable radiobiological modeling is essential to the consistent dosimetric analysis and outcome comparison between conventionally fractionated radiation therapy (CFRT) that employs small daily doses (1.8-4 Gy) and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) that employs large daily doses (> 5 Gy). This work investigates a new radiobiological model, the multimode (MM) model, for both CFRT and SBRT. The MM model assumes the existence of different modes of cell killing because of unsuccessfully repaired radiation damage to the cell deoxyribonucleic acid by any number of ionization events (or radiation tracks). The validity of the MM model was tested using previously published survival fractions of various cell lines. A comparison of the goodness-of-fit of the linear quadratic (LQ), multitarget (MT), universal survival curve (USC) and MM models was made to the survival curve of 12 non-small-cell lung cancer cell line. The same agreement was obtained between the USC and MM models with the survival data, which was significantly better than that with the LQ and MT models. The MM model is a comprehensive model that may offer a superior description of the mammalian cell survival curve in both conventional and ablative dose ranges, which can be used for designing new fractionation schemes and predicting and understanding treatment outcomes for both CFRT and SBRT.

Article.ArticleTitle: Multi-target network modulation of Traditional Chinese Medicine in radiation enteropathy: mechanistic insights and therapeutic implications.

Abstract.AbstractText: Radiation enteropathy (RE) is a common and clinically significant complication of abdominal and pelvic radiotherapy, characterized by multifactorial pathological processes including oxidative DNA damage, epithelial barrier disruption, immune-inflammatory dysregulation, vascular injury, fibrosis, and gut microbiota dysbiosis. Despite its clinical burden, effective disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), widely used in the management of gastrointestinal disorders, has attracted increasing attention as a complementary approach for radiation-induced intestinal injury. Accumulating experimental evidence indicates that TCM formulas, herbal extracts, and bioactive phytochemicals may exert protective effects through coordinated regulation of interconnected pathological processes. Reported protective effects involve several interconnected pathological processes, but the supporting evidence remains uneven. Most studies use acute, single-dose animal models, and many mechanistic conclusions rely on pathway-marker changes rather than functional perturbation. This review therefore evaluates TCM interventions according to disease stage, intestinal site, irradiation design, and the strength of mechanistic support. Multi-target regulation is treated as an interpretive framework rather than a mechanism established for every intervention. Clinical evidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous preparations, inconsistent endpoints, and inadequate follow-up. Translation will require standardized products, clinically relevant fractionated and tumor-bearing models, exposure-relevant mechanistic validation, and rigorous trials that assess intestinal benefit without compromising tumor control.

Article.ArticleTitle: Long-resident ultrasmall zwitterionic nanoparticles normalize vessels and promote photosensitizer accumulation for enhanced photodynamic immunotherapy.

Abstract.AbstractText: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) holds promise for solid tumor treatment but is limited by its oxygen dependence and hypoxia in the tumor microenvironment (TME). Vascular normalization improves perfusion and oxygenation, while the mismatch between the short normalization window and synchronous PDT impairs vascular function, aggravates hypoxia and blunts subsequent vascular normalization. Here, we develop ultra-small zwitterionic nanoparticles (RM-Ce6@St) based on the co-assembly of Ce6-grafted hyperbranched polycarbonates and oxalate ester-linked hyperbranched polycarbonates, encapsulating sunitinib to implement a "multiple accumulation and single irradiation" strategy for enhanced photodynamic immunotherapy. RM-Ce6@St, owing to the small-sized and zwitterionic surface features, exhibits significant tumor accumulation. Subsequently, the ROS-triggered release of sunitinib remodels the vasculature to enhance oxygenation, while long-retained Ce6 allows repeated dosing to cumulatively increase intratumoral Ce6 levels. Consequently, a single irradiation delivered within the normalization window enabled robust ROS generation and markedly improved PDT efficacy. In murine breast cancer models, a single irradiation within the normalization window achieved up to 90.7% tumor growth inhibition, compared with 40.3% for multiple irradiations prior to the window. This "multiple accumulation and single irradiation" further induced immunogenic cell death, promoted dendritic cell maturation, reduced myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration, resulting in potent control of primary and distant tumors.

Article.ArticleTitle: A peptide-based nano-PROTAC synergistically driving ferroptosis-immunotherapy in triple-negative breast cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Ferroptosis, an emerging mechanism of cell death, provides new targets for the treatment of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a key regulator of ferroptosis, is a promising therapeutic target for TNBC. Given that GPX4 is often considered "undruggable", proteolysis targeting chimeras (PROTACs) offer a powerful means for its degradation. However, conventional PROTACs often face challenges in achieving precise localization and potent activation in vivo. Herein, we engineered a peptide-based nano-PROTAC, named CMVG, which couples VHL- and GPX4-binding peptides with iron-based metal-organic frameworks via a "click" reaction and loads the photosensitizer chlorin e6 (Ce6). CMVG enhances ferroptosis through a dual mechanism: it degrades GPX4 via its PROTAC function to initiate ferroptosis, while generating reactive oxygen species under laser irradiation to mediate photodynamic therapy, thereby intensifying oxidative stress and accelerating ferroptosis. Furthermore, the ferroptosis induced by CMVG is highly immunogenic, triggering immunogenic cell death and reshaping the tumor immune microenvironment, ultimately boosting the anti-TNBC immune response. Additionally, CMVG exhibits excellent targeting and biocompatibility, enabling MRI-guided tumor treatment. This work presents the first peptide-based nano-PROTAC for GPX4 degradation, overcoming major limitations of conventional PROTACs, and offers a promising integrated strategy for treating TNBC.

Article.ArticleTitle: A Golgi-Targeted Cu-MOF Nanoplatform Overcomes ATP7B-Mediated Copper Efflux to Amplify Chemo-Cuproptosis Synergy against Colorectal Cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains difficult to treat because of tumor heterogeneity and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Although combining chemotherapy with cuproptosis offers complementary antitumor effects, its efficacy is constrained by poor tumor-selective delivery and ATP7B-associated copper efflux. We developed YC@BS-MOF, a yuanhuacine (YC)-loaded copper metal-organic framework (MOF) with Golgi-targeting capability, to integrate chemotherapy, photodynamic therapy, and cuproptosis. Composed of Cu2+ nodes and Golgi-targeting BS-TCPP photosensitizing ligands, BS-MOF acted as a copper reservoir and, upon light irradiation, induced Golgi disruption that impaired ATP7B-associated Cu handling and promoted intracellular copper retention. Copper retention amplified YC-mediated apoptosis and copper-dependent oxidative stress, leading to enhanced cuproptosis, immunogenic cell death, and activation of the immune microenvironment. Biodistribution analyses showed increased YC tumor accumulation, and in vivo studies demonstrated potent tumor suppression, immune remodeling, and favorable biosafety. This work establishes Golgi-directed regulation of copper trafficking as a subcellular strategy to potentiate chemo-cuproptosis for CRC treatment.

Article.ArticleTitle: Eu-doped gadolinium fluoride nanoparticles as MRI active theranostic agent with pronounced radiocatalytic activity.

Abstract.AbstractText: Radiotherapy remains one of the most widely used and effective methods for tumor treatment. Nanoparticle-based sensitizers are regarded as promising tools in radiotherapy since they can enhance therapeutic efficacy while reducing adverse side effects. Due to their large X-ray absorption cross-section and high proton beam stopping power, lanthanide fluoride nanoparticles have attracted considerable attention as potential radiosensitizers. In this study, we synthesized europium-doped (5, 10 and 20 mass %) gadolinium fluoride nanoparticles (GdEuF3 NPs) and evaluated their radiocatalytic activity under X-ray and proton beam irradiation. Additionally, we performed comprehensive analysis of their cytotoxicity (IC50) and bioactivity using 4 different cell lines (3 cancer and 1 normal cell lines). The synthesized GdEuF3 NPs demonstrated not only high colloidal stability, but also pronounced MRI contrast properties exceeding commercial MRI contrast agents (Gadobutrol®). The GdEuF3 NPs exhibited pH-dependent radiocatalytic activity, which was predominantly observed under acidic conditions (pH 6.5) under proton beam irradiation, while a weaker effect was detected at neutral pH under X-ray irradiation. The GdEuF3 NPs were highly biocompatible with the 4T1, MNNG/Hos, EMT6/P, and NCTC L929 cell lines over a wide concentration range (10-100 μg/mL) and across different europium contents, with no detectable adverse effects. Taking into account the pH-dependent radiation-induced overgeneration of ROS when irradiated with various types of ionizing radiation (photons or protons), the pronounced MRI contrast properties, as well as low cytotoxicity, we can confidently talk about the prospects for their biomedical use as a radiosensitizer in the future.

Article.ArticleTitle: Image-guided photothermal therapy in ovarian cancer using a pH-sensitive ICG/TPZ nanoliposome to overcome thermoresistance.

Abstract.AbstractText: Ovarian cancer remains a lethal gynecological malignancy with limited effective therapies. Photothermal therapy (PTT) is promising but hindered by scarce clinically approved photothermal agents and intrinsic tumor thermoresistance. Herein, we developed a pH-sensitive nanoliposome, ICG@TPZ-Lipo, co-delivering FDA-approved indocyanine green (ICG) and the hypoxia-activated prodrug tirapazamine (TPZ). The liposome exhibited uniform spherical morphology (~50 nm) with a hydrodynamic diameter of ~72 nm (polydispersity index = 0.18). It showed pH-dependent charge reversal from -28.8 to + 2.0 mV when pH value decreased from 7.4 to 5.5. ICG and TPZ loading were 7.3% and 3.4%, respectively. In acidic tumor microenvironment, protonation of poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEOz) triggered disassembly and released > 80% of encapsulated TPZ. Unlike previously reported ICG/TPZ platforms relying on passive co-delivery, our system exploits PEOz-based pH-responsive charge reversal to achieve tumor-acidity-triggered ICG and TPZ tumor accumulation. Under 808 nm laser irradiation, ICG@TPZ-Lipo demonstrated a temperature increase of 17.9 °C with 19.3% photothermal conversion efficiency, and an ability of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Furthermore, ICG@TPZ-Lipo aggravated hypoxia to activate TPZ, causing DNA damage, mitochondrial depolarization, and ATP depletion, which further caused the downregulation of HSF1/HSP90, thereby overcoming thermoresistance. In vitro, ICG@TPZ-Lipo showed superior tumor-cell killing to control nanoparticles. In SKOV3-tumor-bearing mice, ICG@TPZ-Lipo suppressed tumor growth under near-infrared II (NIR-II) fluorescence imaging guidance and achieved complete tumor regression in all treated mice without recurrence. Its therapeutic efficacy was superior than that of the control nanoparticles. Moreover, ICG@TPZ-Lipo demonstrated negligible systemic toxicity. These preclinical findings support further evaluation of this image-guided chemo-photothermal strategy for ovarian cancer.

Article.ArticleTitle: TWIST family in cervical cancer biology: From molecular mechanisms to clinical implications.

Abstract.AbstractText: Despite ongoing clinical efforts, cervical cancer remains one of the most common gynecologic tumors, largely due to its metastatic potential and resistance to chemotherapy. The transcriptional regulator TWIST has been implicated in these features, in part through the induction of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). The expression of TWIST is delicately regulated by several exogenous factors, including hypoxia-driven HIF-1α signaling and TGF-β pathways, as well as endogenous oncogenic cascades such as Wnt/β-catenin, NF-κB, PI3K/Akt, Hedgehog, Notch, and IL-6/JAK2/STAT3. Moreover, the E6 and E7 proteins from high-risk human papillomavirus strains promote TWIST upregulation, facilitating cellular plasticity and evasion of senescence. Post-transcriptional and epigenetic regulation is orchestrated by complex networks of non-coding RNAs and key transcription factors such as Mist1, FOXC1, and LMX-1A. Importantly, hypermethylation of the TWIST1 promoter has been proposed as a candidate biomarker for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. TWIST has been reported to promote tumor-associated phenotypes through E-cadherin downregulation, induction of matrix metalloproteinases, and maintenance of stem cell-like properties. TWIST has been associated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy resistance, potentially through mechanisms involving DNA-damage responses and MDR1/P-glycoprotein-mediated drug efflux. The tumor microenvironment affects its expression and activity, including hypoxia, cancer-associated fibroblasts, inflammatory cytokines, tumor-associated macrophages, and extracellular vesicles. In a clinical context, high levels of TWIST are linked to poor outcomes in cervical cancer. Growing evidence links it to immune evasion through regulation of PD-L1, immunosuppressive cytokine signaling, macrophage polarization, T-cell exclusion, and immune resistance associated with cancer stem cells, underscoring its importance for translation in the current era of immune checkpoint blockade.

Article.ArticleTitle: Synergizing Short-Course Radiotherapy with Immunotherapy in Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: Current Evidence, Challenges, and Future Directions.

Abstract.AbstractText: The management of locally advanced rectal cancer is increasingly moving beyond a uniform cytotoxic framework toward biomarker-informed multimodal treatment. Short-course radiotherapy (SCRT) is an established and convenient radiotherapy option and may also provide an immunomodulatory context for immune checkpoint blockade. Preclinical evidence suggests that hypofractionated radiotherapy can promote immunogenic cell death and modulate the tumor immune microenvironment; however, whether the fractionation schedule of SCRT provides a clinically meaningful immunological advantage over long-course chemoradiotherapy remains uncertain. Early randomized studies of SCRT-based chemoimmunotherapy in predominantly proficient mismatch repair/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) populations have reported encouraging improvements in pathological or overall complete response rates compared with their respective control regimens. Nevertheless, differences in comparator arms, chemotherapy exposure, immunotherapy schedules, endpoint definitions, and follow-up duration preclude firm conclusions regarding the optimal radiotherapy backbone or long-term survival benefit. These findings support further prospective evaluation of SCRT-based combinations and response-adapted non-operative management in appropriately selected patients. Longitudinal circulating tumor DNA, multi-omics profiling, MR-guided adaptive radiotherapy, and computational models such as "digital twins" may contribute to improved patient selection and surveillance, but their clinical utility requires prospective validation.

Article.ArticleTitle: Pulsed Low-dose-rate Radiotherapy Remodels the Tumor Immune Microenvironment and is Associated With Crosstalk Between SPP1⁺ tumor-associated macrophages and GZMK⁺ CD8⁺ T cells.

Abstract.AbstractText: Pulsed low-dose-rate radiotherapy (PLDR) is a promising reirradiation strategy for refractory solid tumors because of its potential to reduce normal tissue toxicity; however, its immunomodulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we retrospectively analyzed clinical outcomes and treatment-related adverse events in 16 patients with refractory solid tumors treated with PLDR. Using MC38 tumor-bearing mice, we compared PLDR and conventional radiotherapy (cRT) under biologically equivalent dose conditions and performed single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize treatment-associated remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIM). Multiplex immunofluorescence staining and spatial analysis were further conducted in an independent cohort of 114 patients with rectal cancer to evaluate the clinical relevance of identified immune features. PLDR achieved comparable local tumor control to cRT while reducing treatment-related toxicity and improving overall survival (OS) in mouse models. In the combination-treatment setting, single-cell analyses showed that PLDR + immunotherapy with an anti-PD-1 antibody combined with the targeted agent anlotinib (ITT), compared with cRT + ITT, was associated with enrichment of Gzmk⁺ CD8⁺ T cells, reduced Spp1⁺ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) abundance, and altered cell-cell communication between these populations. In our independent rectal cancer cohort, the spatial distance between SPP1⁺ TAMs and GZMK⁺ CD8⁺ T cells was independently associated with OS. These findings suggest that the interaction between SPP1⁺ TAMs and GZMK⁺ CD8⁺ T cells may be closely associated with PLDR-related TIM remodeling and may also serve as a potential prognostic biomarker in rectal cancer.

Article.ArticleTitle: Opportunities and Challenges in FLASH Radiotherapy: Focusing on Normal Tissue Protection Effects and Clinical Translation Bottleneck.

Abstract.AbstractText: FLASH radiotherapy (FLASH-RT) has garnered significant attention for its "FLASH effect", which selectively protects normal tissues while maintaining tumor-killing efficacy at ultra-high dose rates (UHDR). This technology represents a promising but still investigational therapeutic strategy in radiation oncology. Since the initial confirmation of the FLASH effect in mouse experiments in 2014, related research has rapidly advanced in key radiation physics parameters, radiation types, and biological mechanisms. However, a lack of consensus on its critical triggering conditions, tissue-specific thresholds, and standardized parameters has hindered its transition from laboratory to clinical application. This review systematically outlines the physical triggering conditions of the FLASH effect, revealing its dependence on a multidimensional combination of parameters including dose rate, single-fraction dose, pulse time structure, and radiation type. It also delves into the underlying multiscale biological mechanisms, encompassing radiochemical aspects such as transient oxygen depletion and free radical kinetics, cellular processes including DNA damage repair and cell death patterns, and systemic changes like immune microenvironment remodeling. It further examines three core challenges hindering FLASH-RT's clinical implementation: technical feasibility and equipment limitations, the complexity and uncertainty of biological mechanisms, and challenges in clinical practice and standardization. This review aims to dissect current research progress and critical issues, providing guidance for advancing FLASH-RT's clinical application.

Journal.Title: The journal of physical chemistry. B

Article.ArticleTitle: Dissociative Electron Attachment in 1,3-Dimethyl-5-Thiocyanatouracil at Different Hydration Conditions.

Abstract.AbstractText: 5-Thiocyanato-2'-deoxyuridine has emerged as a promising radiosensitizer for cancer radiotherapy. Upon X-ray irradiation, hydrated electrons generated in the tumor microenvironment can interact with this molecule, forming reactive transient species capable of inducing damage to DNA, the primary target of radiotherapy. In this work, we investigate dissociative electron attachment (DEA) to 1,3-dimethyl-5-thiocyanatouracil, a doubly methylated analogue of 5-thiocyanato-2'-deoxyuridine, in both the gas phase and microhydrated environments. Gas-phase measurements were performed using a crossed electron-molecular beam apparatus coupled with mass spectrometry, while microhydrated clusters were examined using a CLUster-Beam setup, enabling direct assessment of hydration effects on DEA. The experimental results are supported by quantum chemical calculations, providing insight into thermodynamic and kinetic parameters, including electron affinities, reaction thresholds, and activation barriers. In both environments, the parent anion and the CN- fragment dominate the product distribution, accompanied by minor channels such as SCN- formation. Microhydration leads to a moderate suppression of the S-CN bond cleavage pathway but does not inhibit the reaction. Overall, these findings demonstrate that microhydration modulates, yet preserves, DEA activity in this class of radiosensitizers, supporting their potential effectiveness under biologically relevant conditions.

Article.ArticleTitle: Spatiotemporal control of CAR-T cell TNF release via tumor-targeted irradiation.

Abstract.AbstractText: Adoptive chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies have limited efficacy in solid tumors because of poor infiltration and impaired effector function, whereas radiotherapy is constrained by radioresistance and metastatic spread. Here we show that integrating the spatial precision of ionizing radiation with the biological specificity of CAR-T cells enables localized delivery of the inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF). We identified radiation-responsive genes in tumor-infiltrating T cells and engineered synthetic radioinducible promoters to drive TNF expression. Human CAR-T cells carrying this construct (riTNF CAR-T cells) secreted high levels of TNF upon irradiation, independently of antigen engagement. In human xenograft and murine tumor models, the combination of riTNF CAR-T cells and local irradiation produced greater tumor regression than either treatment alone or standard CAR-T cells with irradiation. This response was associated with high intratumoral, but not systemic, TNF levels, increased tumor necrosis and apoptosis, vascular disruption and greater CAR-T cell infiltration. These findings establish a platform for spatially and temporally controlled cytokine delivery from engineered CAR-T cells.

Article.ArticleTitle: RIG-I is essential for radiation-induced IFN-β production and PD-L1/PD-L2 upregulation in HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells.

Abstract.AbstractText: The RIG-I pathway, a key component of the innate immune system that classically detects cytosolic viral RNA, has also been implicated in regulating tumor cell viability, radiosensitivity, and patient survival across multiple cancer types. However, these effects appear to be context-dependent and partly contradictory. Whether radiotherapy modulates tumor-intrinsic RIG-I signaling in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) depending on HPV status, and whether such modulation is associated with changes in the tumor immune phenotype, remains unknown. Four human HNSCC cell lines (two HPV-negative and two HPV-positive), along with siRNA-mediated RIG-I knockdown and a CRISPR/Cas9-generated RIG-I knockout derivative, were treated with radiotherapy. Tumor cells were analyzed for their immune phenotype, including RIG-I expression via Western blot and flow cytometry, IFN-β secretion via ELISA, and PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression via flow cytometry. Radiotherapy, dose- and fraction-dependent, induced the upregulation of RIG-I expression and IFN-β secretion from HPV-negative HNSCC cells. The knockdown and knockout of the RIG-I-encoding gene DDX58 in the HPV-negative cell line HSC4 minimized both IFN-β secretion and PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression. These effects could be replicated by pre-exposing HPV-negative cell lines to the RIG-I inhibitor RIG012 before irradiation. Interestingly, HPV-positive cells showed less radiotherapy-mediated modulation of RIG-I and of the tumor cell phenotype of immune-related surface markers and showed no significant reaction to the inhibitor treatment. The previously unrecognized RIG-I-IFN-β axis is a central regulator of RT-induced immune checkpoint modulation for HPV-negative HNSCC. These results provide new opportunities to reshape the immune response following RT in HNSCC.

Article.ArticleTitle: Radiation-induced Salivary Gland Fibrosis: Pathogenesis and Potential Targets for Therapeutic Intervention.

Abstract.AbstractText: This review focuses on radiotherapy (RT)-induced salivary gland (SG) fibrosis and current treatment options. Furthermore, we suggest that based on their mechanisms of action, three recently approved anti-fibrotic drugs (namely nintedanib, pirfenidone, and nerandomilast), could be repurposed to treat the fibrosis underlying RT-induced SG hypofunction.

Although saliva substitutes and secretory stimulants are used clinically to relieve symptoms of xerostomia and reduce some of the consequences of hyposalivation, these approaches do not repair underlying damage to SGs due to cancer therapy. Consequently, treatment of salivary hypofunction and xerostomia induced by RT is a major, unmet medical need. The molecular processes underlying RT-induced SG injury culminate in inflammation and oxidative stress associated with SG fibrosis and resultant hyposalivation. Identification of these processes provides potential targets for mechanism-based interventions for treatment of this disorder.

Article.ArticleTitle: Review of radiobiological dose rate effects at the edge between conventional and FLASH.

Abstract.AbstractText: The shift from passive scattering to active pencil beam scanning (PBS) in proton therapy, alongside techniques such as flattening filter-free photon therapy, has increased dose rates in clinical radiotherapy from <0.4 Gy/s to 0.4-35 Gy/s. Meanwhile, ultra-high dose rate radiotherapy (FLASH, ≥40 Gy/s) has emerged as a novel modality that spares normal tissue while maintaining tumor control. Yet, dose rate effects within the 0.4-35 Gy/s range have traditionally been considered negligible. Recent reports of unexpected necroses after proton PBS irradiations challenge this assumption, prompting a reevaluation of potential dose-rate-dependent effects in this intermediate range.This review summarizes current evidence on dose rate effects within 0.4-35 Gy/s, derived from in vivo models (including zebrafish embryos and rodents), in-vitro experiments and water radiolysis studies. Selected experimental and retrospective observations suggest that dose rates in this intermediate range may modify the biological response and, under certain conditions, increase toxicity relative to conventional reference dose rates (<0.4 Gy/s). The magnitude and even direction of dose rate effects appear to depend on radiation quality, total dose, temporal delivery structure, oxygenation, linear energy transfer, tissue type and biological endpoint. The observations described in this review are hypothesis-generating rather than threshold-defining, highlighting the need for further investigation in experimental conditions, preclinical models, and clinical settings.

Article.ArticleTitle: Nano‑platinum-embedded zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 for the enhanced radio-immunotherapy of cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Inorganic ions or inorganic nanoparticles possess unique properties, making them play a significant role in enhancing radiotherapy and immunotherapy for tumor. The development of inorganic biomaterials that can enhance the efficiency of tumor radio-immunotherapy at multiple levels is of great significance for tumor control and requires further exploration. Herein, platinum (Pt) nanoparticles were encapsulated within zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8) nanostructures and ultimately placed in a thermosensitive F127 hydrogel system, obtaining Pt/ZIF@F127 hydrogel for enhancing the tumor radio-immunotherapy. The obtained Pt/ZIF@F127 hydrogel exhibited the characteristics of temperature-responsive gelation, excellent storage stability, acid-triggered zinc ion release and the generation of oxygen upon incubation with hydrogen peroxide. Furthermore, Pt/ZIF@F127 hydrogel amplified the X-ray irradiation-induced DNA damage/immunogenic cell death, and, together with radiotherapy, activated the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes pathway in vitro. After intratumoral injection, this Pt/ZIF@F127 hydrogel could maintain the high content of Zn2+, reduce the content of lactic acid and relieved the hypoxia degree in the tumor tissue, finally realizing the enhanced radio-immunotherapy by enhancement of the radiotherapy effect and optimization of the anti-tumor immune response. Therefore, this study effectively integrates the advantages of multiple inorganic materials, providing relevant biomaterial and strategy for radio-immunotherapy enhancement in cancer treatment.

Article.ArticleTitle: Metabolic stress rewires DHODH from oncogenesis to SLC7A11-driven disulfidptosis and radiosensitization in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

Abstract.AbstractText: Metabolic plasticity enables tumors to adapt to fluctuating nutrient environments, yet the non-canonical functions of metabolic enzymes under stress remain largely unexplored. Here, we established a pyrimidine biosynthesis-associated gene score (PBAGS) that predicts survival in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and identified dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) as a critical driver with a context-dependent dual role. Under glucose-replete conditions, DHODH functions as a canonical oncogene, promoting pyrimidine and cysteine metabolism, alongside UDP-GlcNAc production; accordingly, its inhibition by leflunomide suppresses tumor growth. Strikingly, under glucose starvation, DHODH undergoes a functional switch to become a "molecular executioner." Mechanistically, starvation triggers the DHODH-OGT axis to maintain site-specific O-GlcNAcylation of SLC7A11 at Ser26, thereby stabilizing SLC7A11. This modification promotes excessive cystine accumulation and subsequent actin cytoskeleton collapse, ultimately triggering disulfidptosis. Accordingly, inhibition of DHODH abolishes this modification and rescues cells from starvation-induced death. Clinically, DHODH-SLC7A11 axis correlates tightly with GLUT1 expression. Mimicking glucose starvation using GLUT1 inhibitor BAY-876 significantly enhances radiosensitivity in ESCC PDX models that harbor high DHODH/SLC7A11 expression. Collectively, our findings uncover that under glucose starvation, DHODH and SLC7A11 co-dependency synergistically promotes disulfidptosis, suggesting that targeting the metabolic context offers a potent strategy to sensitize ESCC to radiotherapy.

Journal.Title: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology

Article.ArticleTitle: Linear energy transfer optimization mitigates biological model discrepancies in carbon ion radiotherapy for pelvic osteosarcoma.

Abstract.AbstractText: In the combined treatment of osteosarcoma with a carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) boost, large pelvic tumors are associated with significantly lower tumor control compared to craniofacial localization. This could be linked to lower dose-averaged linear energy transfer (LETd) values in the target and larger uncertainties related to the model used for relative biological effectiveness (RBE) calculation. This study aimed to bridge the difference between RBE-weighted doses from two clinically used models, the local effect model I (LEM-I) and the modified microdosimetric kinetic model (mMKM), using LETd optimization.

Fifteen pelvic osteosarcoma CIRT plans, initially optimized with LEM-I, were re-optimized to achieve higher target LETd while preserving target and organ at risk (OAR) dose objectives. Both dose- and LET-optimized plans were recalculated with mMKM, and dose metrics were compared across the groups. Robustness against setup and range uncertainties and changes in patient anatomy (using control CTs) was investigated.

LETd optimization resulted in target LETd escalation without compromising LEM-I target coverage. The LET-optimized group also demonstrated better mMKM dose coverage and a significant decrease (up to 9% of prescription) in the disparity between LEM-I and mMKM target dose. OAR doses remained largely unaffected by model choice or optimization strategy. The robustness loss with LETd optimization was minor (intra-patient dose variability increased by 0.3-2.3%) compared to the reduction in model-to-model variation.
When adequately balanced with physical uncertainties, LETd optimization could become a useful strategy for bridging RBE model predictions and increasing the efficacy of CIRT.

Article.ArticleTitle: YY1 transcriptionally activates PMVK to promote radioresistance by inhibiting ferroptosis in lung adenocarcinoma.

Abstract.AbstractText: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is a major non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) subtype. Phosphomevalonate kinase (PMVK), a key mevalonate pathway enzyme, promotes LUAD progression. The transcription factor yin yang 1 (YY1) also correlates with LUAD progression; however, their regulatory relationship remains unclear. PMVK was significantly overexpressed in LUAD tissues and radiotherapy-resistant samples; its mRNA and protein levels were higher in the radioresistant (RR) group than in the radiosensitive (RS) group. PMVK knockdown inhibited LUAD cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, elevated ROS, lipid ROS, MDA, and Fe2+ levels, and reduced CoQ10 levels without affecting ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) expression. Under IR, PMVK silencing significantly reduced the survival fraction, increased the proportion of phosphorylated histone H2AX (γ-H2AX) positive cells and elevated apoptosis rates. YY1 directly bound to the PMVK promoter to transcriptionally activate its expression, positively regulating PMVK at both mRNA and protein levels. Transcriptional activation of PMVK by YY1 enhanced LUAD cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, increased the survival fraction, decreased γ-H2AX positive cell ratios and apoptosis rates, lowered ROS, lipid ROS, MDA, and Fe2+ levels, and increased CoQ10 levels, thereby dampening ferroptosis-associated cell death and promoting tumor progression and radiotherapy resistance. Consistently, in vivo xenograft models demonstrated that YY1-mediated PMVK accelerated tumor growth, while simultaneously suppressing DNA damage (γ-H2AX) and lipid peroxidation (4-HNE) induced by irradiation. This study shows that YY1 transcriptionally activates PMVK to modulate radiotherapy resistance and ferroptosis-associated features in LUAD. These findings elucidate LUAD molecular mechanisms and provide a theoretical basis for targeted therapy.

Article.ArticleTitle: RNA 5-Methylcytosine (m5C) in Cancer: An Emerging Epitranscriptomic Hub for Therapy Resistance and Clinical Translation.

Abstract.AbstractText: RNA 5-methylcytosine (m5C) has emerged as an important epitranscriptomic modification in cancer. Rather than acting as a uniformly oncogenic mark, m5C produces context-dependent effects by coupling RNA fate to cellular adaptation. Through control of RNA stability, nuclear export, translation, splicing, and RNA structure, the m5C machinery connects therapeutic stress to DNA damage repair, redox homeostasis, metabolic plasticity, cancer stemness, and tumor-immune interactions. Here, we synthesize the molecular basis of and detection of RNA m5C, distinguish causal from associative evidence, and examine how m5C-dependent RNA regulation contributes to tumor progression and resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy responses. We also discuss tumor-suppressive and context-dependent activities of individual NSUN proteins, cross-talk with other epigenetic and epitranscriptomic pathways, and the methodological limitations that complicate m5C mapping. Current m5C-directed compounds remain preclinical; therefore, their most immediate value lies in mechanistic validation and biomarker development rather than established clinical use. A rigorous, method-aware framework will be essential for determining when m5C is a driver, a permissive adaptation, or a correlate of therapeutic resistance.

Article.ArticleTitle: A Two-Stage Strategy to Reprogram Cyanine Photosensitizers as Controllable-Pyroptosis Inducers for Anticancer Phototherapy.

Abstract.AbstractText: Pyroptosis, a lytic and inflammatory form of programmed cell death, provides a promising strategy for antitumor immunotherapy. However, controllable modulation of pyroptosis using phototherapeutic agents remains challenging. In this study, we report a two-stage molecular reprogramming method to rationally design cyanine photosensitizers with tunable pyroptosis-inducing activity. We first reprogram IR808 into a novel photosensitizer T808, by integrating a tetraphenylethylene unit with IR808, which consequently enhances excited - state features related to intersystem crossing (ISC) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation capability, accompanied by inducing pyroptosis under irradiation. In the second process, T808 is conjugated with poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) chains of varying lengths (M.W. 550, 1000, and 2000 Da) to finely modulate the pyroptotic efficacy. The relationship of PEG chain length with pyroptosis-inducing activity is in the order of PT550 > T808 > PT1000 >> PT2000. Cellular and in vivo studies show that T808, PT550, and PT1000 treatments suppress tumor growth and induce pyroptosis with occurrence of immunogenic cell death (ICD). Even under a lower intratumoral injection dose (25 µM), T808 and PT550 therapies exhibit remarkable antitumor efficacy with measurable pyroptosis features. This work provides a new insight into reprogramming cyanine photosensitizers into pyroptosis-active molecules, and proposes possible structural association of PEGylated cyanines with the pyroptosis activity.

Article.ArticleTitle: Sitagliptin ameliorates radiation-induced oral mucositis by inhibiting oxidative damage and inflammatory response via TLR2/MyD88/NF-κB signaling pathway.

Abstract.AbstractText: Radiotherapy for head and neck cancers is frequently complicated by radiation-induced oral mucositis (RIOM), which can compromise treatment tolerance and negatively affect patients' quality of life. Current preventive and therapeutic options remain limited, highlighting the need for safer and more effective interventions. The development of RIOM involves a cascade of radiation-triggered oxidative stress, epithelial injury, and sustained inflammatory responses. Given the reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities of sitagliptin, a widely used dipeptidyl peptidase - 4 inhibitor, we investigated its potential protective effects against RIOM. Here we show that oral sitagliptin markedly reduces mucosal ulceration and radiation-associated weight loss in mouse models of localized head-and-neck irradiation, while preserving mucosal thickness and basal epithelial stem cells and sustaining proliferative activity after irradiation. Sitagliptin limits reactive oxygen species accumulation and lipid peroxidation, restores glutathione levels and superoxide dismutase activity, and reduces DNA damage, apoptosis, inflammatory cytokine expression, and inflammatory-cell infiltration. Mechanistically, sitagliptin inhibits TLR2/MyD88/NF-κB signaling, whereas pharmacological activation of TLR2 partially reverses its protective effects in vitro, providing further evidence that this pathway contributes to sitagliptin-mediated protection. Sitagliptin is well tolerated in healthy mice, causes no detectable hypoglycemia or organ toxicity, and does not measurably impair radiotherapy-mediated tumor control or tumor radiosensitivity. Collectively, these results demonstrate that sitagliptin protects against RIOM through coordinated antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory actions involving suppression of TLR2/MyD88/NF-κB signaling, while maintaining tumor radiosensitivity. Its established clinical use and the efficacy and tolerability observed in our preclinical models support further evaluation of sitagliptin for RIOM.

Article.ArticleTitle: Identification of EI-17056 as a novel small-molecule radiosensitizer in parental H460 and radioresistant H460R lung cancer cells.

Abstract.AbstractText: Radiotherapy is a major treatment modality for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, acquired radioresistance remains a significant challenge that limits its therapeutic efficacy. Therefore, we aimed to evaluate our in-house chemical library of heterocycle-based compounds spanning diverse chemical scaffolds to identify molecules capable of enhancing radiation responsiveness in lung cancer cells, including those with acquired radioresistance. Briefly, H460 cells were subjected to repeated fractionated irradiation (2 Gy per fraction) at a cumulative dose of 80 Gy to generate a radioresistant H460 subline (H460R). The radioresistant phenotype was confirmed by clonogenic survival, Annexin V apoptosis, and intracellular oxidative signal assays following irradiation. Subsequently, a library of 59 structurally diverse heterocycle-based small molecules was screened in H460 and H460R cells. Among the compounds tested, EI-17056, a benzylpyrazole scaffold, was identified as a lead radiosensitizing candidate and exhibited minimal cytotoxicity when administered alone under the screening conditions. Pretreatment with EI-17056 enhanced radiation-induced cell death, as demonstrated by clonogenic survival and Annexin V apoptosis assays. Furthermore, EI-17056 increased intracellular oxidative signals and γH2AX levels following irradiation in both H460 and H460R cells. Importantly, treatment with N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC) attenuated the EI-17056-associated increase in intracellular oxidative signals and reduced the enhancement of radiation-induced apoptosis, providing functional evidence that oxidative stress contributes, at least in part, to EI-17056-enhanced radiation-induced cell death. Collectively, our findings identify EI-17056 as a novel small-molecule radiosensitizing candidate that enhances radiation responsiveness in parental H460 cells and shows encouraging evidence of radiosensitizing activity in acquired radioresistant H460R cells. These results support further investigation of EI-17056 as a candidate therapeutic radiosensitizer, while its broader applicability to NSCLC remains to be established in additional models.

Article.ArticleTitle: Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy and immunotherapy in metastatic colorectal cancer: overcoming immune resistance through immune priming.

Abstract.AbstractText: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are effective in the approximately 5% of metastatic colorectal cancers (mCRC) that are microsatellite instability-high or mismatch repair-deficient (MSI-H/dMMR), whereas microsatellite-stable or mismatch repair-proficient (MSS/pMMR) disease rarely responds to ICI monotherapy. Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) has been proposed to prime antitumor immunity in MSS disease. Preclinical studies show that high-dose-per-fraction radiation can induce immunogenic cell death, release tumor antigens and activate the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway, which may increase T-cell infiltration and, in some models, cause regression of non-irradiated lesions (the abscopal effect). Clinical data come mainly from small, single-arm, early-phase studies that report acceptable safety but modest response rates, and no colorectal-specific randomized trial has shown a survival benefit from adding SABR to immunotherapy. This review summarizes the biological rationale, critically appraises the clinical evidence, including chemo-immuno-radiotherapy in rectal cancer, and discusses toxicity, patient selection, dose-fractionation and sequencing. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from January 2000 to February 2026. SABR-induced immune priming in MSS mCRC is biologically plausible but should be tested in biomarker-stratified randomized trials.
