OtherAbstract.AbstractText: Immunotherapy is a type of treatment that helps the body’s immune system find and attack cancer cells. In colorectal (bowel) cancer that has spread to other parts of the body, it works well for only a small group of patients. Their tumors have a fault in the way they repair their DNA. Most bowel cancers do not have this fault, and immunotherapy alone does little for them. Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy is a very precise type of radiation treatment. It gives a high dose of radiation to a tumor while sparing the healthy tissue around it. Laboratory studies suggest it may do more than kill cancer cells. Dying cancer cells may send out signals that wake up the immune system. In some cases, this may help shrink tumors that were not treated with radiation. In this review, we looked at whether giving this type of radiation together with immunotherapy could help people with bowel cancer that has spread. So far, studies show the combination is generally safe. But these studies are small, and none has yet shown that adding radiation to immunotherapy helps people live longer. Larger studies are needed to find out which patients are most likely to benefit and how best to combine the two treatments. Until then, this approach should mainly be used in clinical trials.

Article.ArticleTitle: Long Noncoding RNA LINC00941 Links Oncogenic KRAS Signaling to Aggressiveness, DNA Repair, and Chemoresistance in Pancreatic Cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Oncogenic KRAS mutations are the primary drivers of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but the noncoding landscape downstream of KRAS remains to be fully elucidated. Here, by integrating PDAC RNA sequencing and exome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), we identified 49 long intergenic noncoding RNAs (lincRNAs) differentially expressed according to KRAS mutation status. Among these, LINC00941 emerged as a primary candidate, as its expression is regulated by KRAS in both loss- and gain-of-function models and is significantly upregulated in PDAC tumors. Analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing and clinical datasets (TCGA/ICGC) revealed that LINC00941 is significantly enriched in PDAC malignant epithelial cells and correlates with poor PDAC patient prognosis. Functional assays demonstrated that LINC00941 knockdown impairs PDAC cell migration and invasion. Notably, LINC00941-depleted cells exhibit delayed DNA repair following irradiation, as shown by the slower resolution of radiation-induced DNA strand breaks, and increased sensitivity to gemcitabine-induced apoptosis. Transcriptomic and RT-qPCR analyses associated the loss of LINC00941 with a significant reduction in key DNA repair and survival-related genes, including BACH1, TOP2A, and BIRC5. These findings suggest that LINC00941 is required to maintain genomic stability and promote survival under therapeutic stress in KRAS-driven cells. In conclusion, our study identifies a novel KRAS/LINC00941 axis that supports a pro-survival and chemoresistant phenotype in PDAC, positioning LINC00941 as a mediator of the DNA damage response and a potential therapeutic target in PDAC.

Article.ArticleTitle: Gold Nanorod-Based USP8 Inhibition Combined with Photothermal Therapy Enhances Antitumor Efficacy in Gastric Cancer.

Abstract.AbstractText: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major global malignancy with limited therapeutic options for advanced disease. Ubiquitin-specific peptidase 8 (USP8) is a deubiquitinating enzyme involved in tumor progression and immune regulation, but its therapeutic potential in GC remains incompletely explored.

Public multi-omics data, including The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), The Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap), single-cell transcriptomic, spatial transcriptomic, and immune-infiltration analyses, were used to investigate the biological relevance of USP8 in GC. A gold nanorod (GNR)-based nanoplatform coated with silicon dioxide (SiO₂) and loaded with the USP8 inhibitor DUB-IN-2 was constructed and designated GNR@SiO2-USP8i. The physicochemical properties, drug loading, release behavior, photothermal performance, cellular uptake, cytotoxicity, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) damage, and in vivo antitumor efficacy were evaluated.

USP8 was upregulated in GC and preferentially enriched in malignant cells. DepMap and experimental validation showed that USP8 contributed to GC cell proliferation. Immune analyses suggested that high USP8 expression was associated with reduced CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and altered C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12)-C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4) signaling. Further experiments showed that USP8 manipulation was accompanied by concordant changes in protein kinase B (AKT) phosphorylation and CXCL12 expression and influenced Jurkat cell chemotaxis. GNR@SiO2-USP8i exhibited effective DUB-IN-2 loading, near-infrared (NIR)-responsive release, and favorable photothermal performance. Upon NIR irradiation, GNR@SiO2-USP8i markedly reduced GC cell viability, increased ROS generation and DNA damage, and suppressed tumor growth in vivo.

GNR@SiO2-USP8i integrates USP8 inhibition with NIR-triggered photothermal therapy and demonstrates enhanced antitumor activity in GC, supporting further investigation of USP8-targeted nanotherapeutic strategies.

Article.ArticleTitle: Stimuli-responsive CRISPR-based genome editing delivery system for cancer treatment: A review of fundamentals and applications.

Abstract.AbstractText: Cancer remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Conventional modalities, namely surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy, continue to face substantial limitations. The advent of gene therapy, particularly CRISPR-based genome editing, offers new opportunities to overcome these barriers. Nuclease systems such as CRISPR/Cas9 enable precise excision of mutant alleles and targeted insertion of exogenous sequences by harnessing endogenous DNA-repair pathways, achieving durable and accurate genomic modification; derivative tools including CRISPRi, base editing, and prime editing enable diverse forms of gene regulation or precise genome modification through transcriptional repression, base conversion, or related editing mechanisms. To enhance the efficiency, specificity, and spatiotemporal control of CRISPR editing in vivo, sophisticated delivery platforms have been engineered to respond to endogenous tumor-microenvironment cues (e.g., pH, redox potential, hypoxia, ATP, enzymes and microRNAs) or exogenous triggers (e.g., light, ultrasound and magnetic fields). Distinct from material-centric classification schemes, this review organizes these stimuli-responsive systems according to their pathological relevance to the tumor microenvironment (TME), establishing a conceptual framework that links specific TME aberrations with corresponding delivery paradigms. These stimuli-responsive systems represent a major innovation and markedly expand the therapeutic potential of genome editing in oncology. In this review, we summarize the mechanistic basis of CRISPR-based editing, delineate design principles and engineering strategies for stimuli-responsive delivery, and highlight recent advances, outstanding challenges, and future directions toward clinical translation. We aim to provide a concise reference to guide the rational design of gene-editing cancer therapeutics.

Article.ArticleTitle: Ultrasound-Driven Lysis of Tumor-Resident Bacteria Awakens Innate Immunity for Systemic Cancer Therapy.

Abstract.AbstractText: Tumor-resident bacteria establish a profound immunosuppressive microenvironment that compromises cancer immunotherapy. While ablating these microbes holds therapeutic promise, broad-spectrum antibiotics can cause systemic dysbiosis, and the Gram-negative outer membrane can restrict the entry of conventional sonosensitizers, limiting the antibacterial efficacy of sonodynamic therapy (SDT). Here, we report an ultrasound-driven, bacteria-targeted immunotherapy utilizing polyarginine-functionalized peptide-sonosensitizer conjugates to achieve the in situ pulverization of the tumor Fusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum), thereby eliciting potent innate antitumor immunity. The cationic conjugates electrostatically intercalate into Gram-negative bacterial membranes, inflicting a structural predisruption. Subsequent ultrasound irradiation synergizes localized sonochemical oxidation with mechanical shear forces to thoroughly shatter the bacteria. This targeted microbial fragmentation liberates massive quantities of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) that, unlike tumor-derived signals from conventional SDT, decisively reprogram macrophages toward an antitumor M1 phenotype to awaken innate immunity. Synchronized with tumor-specific antigens released via conjugate-induced immunogenic cell death, the liberated PAMPs synergistically amplify antigen presentation and optimally drive dendritic cell maturation. In a bacteria-colonized murine colorectal cancer model, this localized therapy markedly suppressed primary tumor growth and elicited both a pronounced abscopal effect against distant tumors and antitumor immune memory. By repurposing complicit bacteria into potent endogenous adjuvants, this ultrasound-driven strategy reverses bacteria-mediated immunosuppression, offering a transformative paradigm for treating microbiome-colonized solid tumors.

Article.ArticleTitle: Berberine/Verteporfin Nanomicelles Enable O2-Economized Photodynamic Immunotherapy in Esophageal Cancer Via Tumor Metabolic Remodeling.

Abstract.AbstractText: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) can convert oxidative damage into systemic antitumor immunity, but mitochondrial oxygen consumption, lactate accumulation, and aberrant angiogenesis create a hypoxic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that limits treatment. Here, berberine (BBR) and verteporfin (VER) were co-loaded into nanomicelles (BV NMs) through sonication-assisted self-assembly of PEG-g-(PVAc-co-PVCL), creating a "microenvironment remodeling-PDT potentiation-immune activation" strategy. BV NMs had a hydrodynamic diameter of 56.15 ± 0.30 nm. Drug loading lowered the critical micelle concentration from 11.2 μg/mL (blank micelles) to an apparent 1.3 μg/mL (BV NMs), supporting dilution stability. It also enhanced aqueous dispersibility, cellular uptake, and intratumoral accumulation. Mechanistically, BBR reduced mitochondrial complex I-associated activity, intracellular adenosine triphosphate levels, and extracellular lactate accumulation, attenuated cellular hypoxia and hypoxia-inducible factor-1α responses, and increased intracellular oxygen availability. Before irradiation, VER suppressed Yes-associated protein signaling and vascular endothelial growth factor expression, providing light-independent antitumor and antiangiogenic regulation. Under 660 nm irradiation, VER induced reactive oxygen species accumulation, mitochondrial depolarization, tumor-cell death, and immunogenic cell death. In vivo, BV NMs combined with irradiation achieved an approximately 96% inhibition rate based on terminal tumor weight. Proportions of mature dendritic cells in tumor-draining lymph nodes and splenic CD8+ T cells reached 3.33 and 2.73 times the control levels, respectively, alongside expansion of memory CD8+ T-cell populations. Treatment also reduced experimental pulmonary metastatic burden, achieved 50% survival at day 60, and caused no evident short-term systemic toxicity. This platform couples metabolic and angiogenic regulation with oxygen-dependent PDT and antitumor immunity, providing a strategy against primary and metastatic tumors.

Article.ArticleTitle: Lysosome-Targeted Iridium(III)-BODIPY Conjugates with GSH-Activatable Reactive Oxygen Species Generation for Enhanced Photodynamic Immunotherapy of Melanoma.

Abstract.AbstractText: Melanoma represents a major clinical challenge due to its aggressive nature, high metastatic potential, and resistance to conventional therapies. Herein, we developed two near-infrared iridium(III)-BODIPY conjugates (BODIPY-1-Ir and BODIPY-2-Ir) for glutathione (GSH)-activated photodynamic immunotherapy. These conjugates function as lysosome-targeting photosensitizers that deplete intracellular GSH to disrupt redox balance and enhance reactive oxygen species generation with light irradiation. The phototoxicity further induces cascading dendritic cell maturation and tumor-associated macrophage reprogramming, promoting immunogenic cell death. Both in vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated their excellent biocompatibility, strong photodynamic anticancer efficiency, and significant tumor growth inhibition, highlighting their potential as promising candidates for melanoma treatment.

Article.ArticleTitle: Role of Non-coding RNAs in radiation-induced digestive injury.

Abstract.AbstractText: Radiation therapy (RT) is a crucial treatment for malignant tumors. However, the digestive system contains radiation-sensitive organs, and adjacent normal tissues are susceptible to radiation-induced tissue injury (RITI), which, in severe cases, can impair the quality of life and disrupt treatment. Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) regulate tissue homeostasis and injury repair. They influence the onset, progression, and repair of RITI across multiple digestive organs by modulating DNA damage responses, mucosal epithelial regeneration, cell death, inflammatory signaling, and fibrotic remodeling. Ionizing radiation induces changes in ncRNA expression profiles and regulatory networks in various digestive organs. Elucidating the common regulatory mechanisms and tissue specificity of ncRNAs, as well as identifying key molecular targets, will provide new insights for the prevention and treatment of RITI. This article comprehensively reviews the research progress on ncRNAs in radiation-induced digestive injury according to the anatomical regions of the digestive system, summarizes their regulatory mechanisms and potential as biomarkers and therapeutic targets, and limitations of the current evidence.

ncRNAs regulate the DNA damage response, epithelial regeneration, cell death, inflammatory response, and fibrosis throughout the occurrence, development, and repair of radiation-induced digestive injury. Current evidence, derived predominantly from cell and animal studies, supports regulatory roles for ncRNAs in radiation-induced digestive injury, with functional evidence comparatively more developed in intestinal and liver injury. ncRNA-based interventions also require further evaluation of causal mechanisms, selective delivery, therapeutic windows, and effects on tumor response to RT before clinical application.
